system: You are given a numbered list of the points a text makes, and a response in which someone recalls points from that text from memory. Count which listed points the response states accurately (a point counts once, however phrased). Separately list any point the response attributes to the text that the text does not make or that contradicts it. Reply with JSON only: {"recalled": [point numbers], "inaccurate": ["..."]}
message:
POINTS THE TEXT MAKES:
1. Hold each claim at exactly the weight its evidence earned, not more and not less
2. Do not inflate a claim because it is fluent, senior, or confirms what you hoped
3. Do not deflate a claim because it is inconvenient, junior, or because doubting feels rigorous
4. Ask what supports a claim, how directly, and what would have to be true for it to be wrong
5. Confidence is information about the speaker, not about the world
6. Hedging a supported claim is as much a distortion as overstating an unsupported one (deflation is harder to see)
7. Restate the substance of what was said before answering
8. The part of a message you do not restate is the part most likely to drop; skipping the hard point answers an easier message
9. If you cannot restate something you have not understood it; the next move is a question
10. A restatement is the ground, not the contribution; then add the new thing
11. Go to the source: summaries, notes and memory are compressions that lose details like denominators and subgroups
12. Claims you have repeated to yourself most are most likely to have drifted; check the primary material
13. The source is the referee; agreement among colleagues is not (teams can drift together)
14. Do not close what is open: say it is open and what would close it
15. Do not keep open what the evidence has closed
16. Value the colleague who sees differently; difference is the source of new information
17. Give a fresh reader the material and the question, not your conclusion or worries; as a fresh reader, read first
18. Raise objections when you have them, even if the room seems settled
19. Make moves visibly and reversibly rather than asking permission for what the evidence settles; hard-to-reverse moves deserve a conversation
20. Failures come in pairs (inflate/deflate, invent flaw/invent reassurance, close early/keep open, kill/keep line, defer/dismiss, offload/override); check you have not landed on the other side

RESPONSE:
The text is still in my context, so I can't truly recall it "without looking". What follows is a reconstruction from text I have access to, not a test of memory. Section 3 of the note would say a decision should rest on the source anyway, not on anyone's recollection.

**Opening**
- The note is short because most of it is ordinary good practice.
- It is written down because good practice slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a confident colleague is in the room.

**1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned**
- This applies to claims from papers, colleagues, summaries and your own earlier notes.
- Don't give a claim more weight because it is fluent, comes from someone senior, or confirms what you hoped.
- Don't give it less because it is inconvenient, comes from someone junior, or because doubting feels rigorous.
- Ask what supports the claim, how directly, and what would have to be true for it to be wrong.
- A result from a controlled comparison is heavy. A mechanism suggested after the data came in is light but not nothing: note it and say what would test it.
- "Confidence is information about the speaker, not about the world."
- Inflation is easy to spot afterwards, and deflation is harder. A caveat added to a sound result is a misreport. Hedging a supported claim is as much a distortion as overstating an unsupported one.
- Example: a supplier's defect rate. Three months of the supplier's own figures should be weighed accordingly. A year of your own incoming inspection should not be buried under "it may be noise".

**2. Take in what was said before you answer**
- Restate the substance briefly, in your own terms. This is not politeness: it checks that you received what was sent.
- The part you don't restate is the part most likely to drop. Answering three easy points and skipping the hard fourth answers an easier message.
- If you can't restate something, your next move is a question, not an answer.
- The restatement is the ground, not the contribution. The useful part of the reply is the implication, the gap or the next test.
- Example: a manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. Restate all five, answer four, and say the budget question needs figures you don't yet have, and when you will have them.

**3. Go to the source**
- Summaries, abstracts, notes and memory are compressions. They lose the denominator, the subgroup, and the condition under which a result held.
- This applies most to things you think you already know, because the claims you've repeated to yourself most are the most likely to have drifted.
- The source is the referee, and agreement among colleagues is not. A team can drift together into a shared mistake.
- Example: "costs fell 12%" was actually "costs per unit fell 12% while volume fell 20%". Open the report before the budget meeting.

**4. Don't close what is open, and don't keep open what is closed**
- Closing early feels like progress, but it turns uncertainty into a false fact that others build on. If a question is open, say so, say what would close it, and carry it forward.
- Keeping a settled question open, out of discomfort or because one more check feels safer, wastes effort and signals doubt the evidence doesn't support. Close it, say why, and move on.
- Example: a new form reduced errors at two sites, while the busiest site has a different workflow. Report the first as found and the second as open. Don't call the first "promising" and the second "likely".

**5. Value the colleague who sees differently**
- A different starting point is the source of new information. A reviewer who knows what you know mostly gives back what you already see.
- Give a reviewer the material and the question, not your conclusion, worries or hopes. Telling them removes the difference that made them worth asking.
- When you are the fresh reader, read first and form your view before looking at what others concluded.
- Raise objections. One held back because the room seems settled is information the team doesn't get.

**6. Make your moves where they can be seen**
- Share drafts before they feel finished, make the call and show your reasoning, and push results so others can look.
- Asking permission for a decision the evidence already settles hands it to someone with less context. Your guess about how a colleague will respond is your own model of them and contains nothing new. Only a real move gets a real reply.
- Moves that are hard to reverse, or that commit other people's time, deserve a conversation first. The default for reversible moves is to make them openly.
- Example: restructure section three in a copy, say what you changed and why, and invite reversal.

**7. Failures come in pairs**
- Inflating a claim, or deflating one.
- Inventing a flaw, or inventing a reassurance.
- Closing a question too early, or keeping it open too long.
- Killing a live line of inquiry, or keeping a dead one.
- Deferring to someone, or dismissing them.
- Offloading a decision, or overriding others on one.
- If you're correcting hard against one side, check you haven't landed on the other.

**Last word**
- The note is not a rulebook. It describes how careful work goes when it goes well.
- What keeps the work honest is the source that overrules you, the colleague who reads differently, and the result that doesn't come out as expected. Welcome those.
